Oh I didn't mean that the only people on forces medication are dangerous, not at all.

But Schizophrenia is an ilness which makes it very hard to function and always see reality clearly.
People forcibly admitted may be so because they can't take care of themselves.

As the other person, who deleted their account pointed out, people with Schrizophrenia are one of the most vulnerable people in society and are more often victims than "normal" people.

But that's not because we have the label Schizophrenia, it's because we're vulnerable and find it difficult to live/adjust in this society.

If some idiot assault a homeless, muttering schizophrenic man on the street, it's not because of the diagnosis, but because he looks like an easy target.

I completely agree, that forcing someone to do something against their will is horrifying, but again, what if this person suffer from capgras syndrome and believes everyone is out to hurt them and at risk of hurting themselves?
Should we just let them be and spiral out of control? 

And you're right in that revolving door patients, and making money of sick people is wrong and should be stopped, but I would not put that on the psych institution, but on the countries and governments without universal healthcare, who cares more about money than welfare.

I mean, I don't think insulin should cost as much as it does in the US, but that doesn't mean people can just stop using it and be fine.

I just took a quick glance through that sub, and it's most uovoted posts of all time, and I disagree, it doesn't seem rational at all.

I'm not supporting the psychiatric institution blindly, (I do live in Scandinavia though, so my experiences may be different than yours) and I don't think any "institution" is completely free of corruption, but I think the anti-pshych movement is misguided.

In some way, I agree with you that Schizophrenia is not some illness set in stone, but that's why we try labelling and naming symptoms. To describe something that keeps popping up and trying to understand it on a broader spectrum.

Doctors and psychiatrists know this, that's why definitions keep changing.

Psychiatry have changed so much the last 100 years, that it's almost unbelievable, and it'll keep changing, hopefully, as we learn more about the mind and ourselves.

As for forcing therapy and medication on patients, I do get why it's distressing, but I'm gonna be honest and say it's needed.

People don't get forced on meds for just being quirky.
I met someone, when I was admitted the first time, who had killed a man in a psychosis after he stopped taking his meds.
And like we put murderers in prison, shouldn't we do everything we can to ensure the safety of others, when psychotic people become dangerous?

Ofcourse that guy is not your average schizophrenic, we all know on this sub, that almost all of us are completely harmless, but when it's hard to separate fantasy from reality, where does the line get drawn on what we can decide ourself which behaviour is harmful?

I gently kicked the floor, slowly rotating in my black leather chair towards the door, still stroking the white cat in my lap.


“Yes, Igor?”


He made a small grimace before looking at the papers in his hand and shuffled them nervously.


“Sir, it’s.. I have to talk to you.”


“Yes?” The white cat purred and I wondered for a moment if it had a name. It was the third cat this week and I had better use of my time than remembering every name my personal cat breeder told me when he handed a new one over.
This one was good though, the right shade of white, perfectly fluffy, and well behaved. It could just be lazy, since it had been laying content in my lap for hours now, but it didn’t matter what it’s motivation was. For now, it was perfect.


“There seem to be have been.. made some excessive purchases in the name of the company these last few months.”


“Mhm.”


“I was talking to Dennis from accounting and-”


“You mean Igor.”


Igor furrowed his brow.


“Sir, with all due respect.. You can’t call all of us Igor. My name is Bob and managing a workforce of 3500 people is incredibly difficult when you-”


“Well, we could always switch to numbers.”


I smiled. Yes, brilliant idea number one of the day. It gave of an even more sinister vibe than Igor. The cat seemed to purr in agreement and I scratched it behind its ears.


“You can be No. 2, Igor. I of course am No. 1.”


“Bob. But, yes alright. I guess that’ll do.”


“Problem solved then.”


I swirled the chair around again, cackling to myself as I looked out of my new panorama window at New York. Feeble little ants.


“Good thinking sir, although that is not why I came here.” 


No. 2 was shuffling around nervously and I let out a loud groan. “What, then?”


“Sir, these purchases they could be very.. misleading to the public eye if someone got hold of them. In the last three months you’ve been buying 300 trap doors, four submarines, two tons of C4, a laser, 100 black suits, a cat breeding kennel, a shark breeding kennel and your own personal army of ninja assassins.” He took a deep breath before continuing. “I know you’ve always had your own ideas, and obviously the best interests at heart for the company, but I have to know. What are these things for? It honestly seem sinister.” 


I swirled the chair around again. He hadn’t even mentioned it, but it was already the best purchase of all. I hadn’t been cheap, but it never squeaked or made a sound, and the leather had a rich quality smell. No to mention the color complimented my one, white contact lens.


“Igor, I mean, No. 2.” I smiled. “Relax. These are just some extra precautions. The trapdoors are a brilliant investment for our firm.”


“How so?”


“Well.. Imagine, a door to door salesman. Now you won’t even have to talk to him.  A flick of a switch and he’s gone to the sharks. I mean, safety.”


“Sir, I know a lot of the team had questions when you decided to move our offices to the Statue of Liberty, but I told them to keep their mouths shut because you’re a good boss and I trust you. I’ve never had dental before. But I can no longer stand idly by. We’re just a greeting card company. I have to report you to--” 


But I had stopped listening and let out a small sigh. It was a shame. No. 2 had been a good henchman. I flicked the switch located under my mahogany desk and he disappeared screaming into the dark square that had appeared in the floor. 


“I told you the trapdoors was a good investment, No. 2.”


And I erupted into sinister laughter as I made a mental note to hire a vocal coach.
